t: Visa Pillaiyar, Visakha Pillaiyar, IBC Pillaiyar
b:
One of the deep-rooted landmarks of Wellawatte is the Visa Pillaiyar. Just as they say you can't trace the origin of a sage, I still haven't got hold of Pillaiyar's origin either. One story passed down by word of mouth says he floated in on the tsunami. But a post I read recently said he was there even before that. There are many stories of gods that floated in on the tsunami. Perhaps that tale was stretched to include him too. Apparently he also has the name "Tsunami Pillaiyar". Another grandmother told me that when the tsunami came it passed by without touching him. Only Pillaiyar himself knows.

Many of today's generation know him only as the Visakha Pillaiyar. They are unlikely to know the story of how "Visa" became "Visakha". It was a time when people fled the country during the war. Everyone who spent their days waiting knows the worth of the Visa Pillaiyar. Every Friday the temple would be terribly crowded. I forgot to tell you about the temple's layout. Let's take a quick look at the temple and come back.

It is a small temple. The Murikandy Pillaiyar is far better off. He squats in a cramped little spot, facing the sea. Beside him, Nagathambiran. That's the whole temple. Now Kathirgama Kandan has newly taken shelter next to him. Outside, past the gate, there are the camphor plate, holy ash, sandal paste and kumkum. In the morning, abhishekam and puja. In the evening, decoration and puja. Friday is very special. Modakam, aval, kozhukattai, chickpeas: offerings pile up. While we stand gazing at all of it with longing, they open the lid, wave the lamp before Pillaiyar, sprinkle water, and the puja ends. After that, while Pillaiyar sits all alone, the people of Wellawatte, regardless of race or religion, jostle for the prasadam. Since I've been a customer since I was small, I don't jostle; I stand to one side like Kirasambal, and the prasadam reaches me anyway.

But wait. In just this way, in those days every visa approval would pile up like prasadam. That is how Pillaiyar became the "Visa Pillaiyar". Later, as the country prospered and fewer people needed visas, Pillaiyar became the "Visakha Pillaiyar". But the devotion and the power did not diminish. Even I, when I couldn't get a tourist visa for Vietnam, dropped 50 rupees in the hundi, prayed, and got the visa (that someone else's visa then went wrong, and he was sent along as company for me when I was about to go alone, is another story).

The street Pillaiyar sits on is called IBC Road. It gets that name because the International Buddhist Centre is there. So Pillaiyar became the "IBC Pillaiyar" too. It's just like the story of the Pillaiyar on Vajira Road, where the Vajiraramaya temple is, becoming the "Vajira Pillaiyar". There seems to be some bond between the Buddha and Pillaiyar. Perhaps it's because both, wanting no trouble, went off on their own to sit under a peepal tree.

Even today he is the refuge of the Wellawatte community. Even though many new ones have risen, Anjaneyar, Amman, Lord Shiva, and big agamic temples have grown, a community still lives on that begins everything with him: birthdays, journeys, the new year.

As an extension of that community, I too,

stand praying to the pure gem with the noble elephant face...
note: Pillaiyar is the Tamil name for Ganesha. Murikandy Pillaiyar is the famous roadside temple on the A9 highway to Jaffna. Nagathambiran is a serpent deity; Kathirgama Kandan is Murugan of Kataragama. Modakam, aval and kozhukattai are offerings of sweets and rice flakes; prasadam is food blessed and shared after worship. Both Ganesha and the Buddha are traditionally found under the peepal tree. The last line quotes Avvaiyar's invocation to Ganesha.
